en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Bhūtagāma-vagga 20.
The Training Rule on Living Beings.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Now at that time, the monks of Āḷavī, while performing construction work, knowingly sprinkled water containing living beings onto grass and clay, or had it sprinkled.
Those monks who were few in desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
"How can these monks of Āḷavī knowingly sprinkle water containing living beings onto grass and clay, or have it sprinkled?"
Then those monks, having rebuked the monks of Āḷavī in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ...“Is it true, monks, that you knowingly sprinkle or cause grass or clay to be sprinkled with water containing living beings?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, knowingly sprinkle even grass or clay with water containing living beings, or cause others to do so?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so forth].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
“Whosoever, monk, knowingly sprinkles water containing living beings upon grass or clay, or causes it to be sprinkled, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, moreover:
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"Knows" means either he knows by himself, or others inform him.
"He should pour" means...
If she sprinkles herself, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"If she causes another to sprinkle" means that if she commands another, there is an offense of expiation.
If, having been instructed once, he sprinkles even a large amount, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If there are living beings and he perceives them as such, and he sprinkles grass or clay, or causes it to be sprinkled, it is an offense of expiation.
If there are living beings and he is doubtful about them, and he sprinkles grass or clay, or causes it to be sprinkled, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If there are living beings, but he perceives them as being without living beings, and he sprinkles grass or clay, or causes it to be sprinkled, there is no offense.
If there are no living beings, but he perceives them as having living beings, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If there are no living beings, but he is uncertain about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is a living being and he perceives it as a living being, there is no offense.
There is no offense if it was unintentional.
for one who is lacking mindfulness,
for one who is ignorant,
for one who is insane,
"For one who is a first-time offender.
The tenth training rule concerning water containing living beings is finished.
The second chapter on plants and seeds is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Regarding what has occurred, knowing, complaining,
and those two who depart.
"Previously, having been driven out,
and [having struck] the door with a living being."
